captions: Chapter four — the price chart, the tools,
and where to find genuine research.
Fundamentals tell you WHAT to buy.
Technicals help with WHEN.
And knowing the right sources keeps you learning from teachers,
not from tip-sellers.
Let's cover all three.
Technical analysis is the study of the price chart.
It doesn't tell you what a company is worth —
it tells you what the crowd is doing, which helps with timing.
Four basics.
The first is trend — simply the direction.
A series of higher highs and higher lows is an uptrend.
The trader's first rule is: don't fight the trend.
Don't try to catch a falling knife.
The second is support and resistance.
Support is a price floor where buyers repeatedly step in.
Resistance is a ceiling where sellers repeatedly appear.
These levels are where the action happens.
The third is volume — how many shares changed hands.
Volume is the conviction behind a move.
A big price move on strong volume is real; a move on thin volume is suspect.
The fourth is moving averages,
which smooth out the daily noise to reveal the true direction.
When the fifty-day average crosses above the two-hundred-day,
traders call it a golden cross — a classic sign of strength.
A final caution: technicals are probabilities, not prophecy.
The chart shows the past.
Use it humbly.
Where do you actually do this research?
A toolkit — and the good news is the best tools are free.
Start with Screener dot in.
It gives you a company's financials, its filings,
and lets you build custom screens — for example,
all companies with return on equity above fifteen and debt below one.
It is the beginner's best friend.
Next, platforms like Tickertape and Trendlyne add clean ratios,
quality scores, foreign and domestic investor flows,
the results calendar, and broker reports in one place.
But the single most valuable source is primary: the company's own annual report and its quarterly concall transcript.
This is management speaking in their own words.
Reading a few of these teaches you more than a hundred videos.
And for the ground truth — official filings, announcements,
order wins — go straight to the NSE, BSE, and SEBI websites.
When in doubt, check the source.
Now, where should you learn —
the popular channels people actually trust.
Present all of these as teachers of concepts,
not sources of tips.
For structured learning from absolute zero,
the gold standard is Zerodha Varsity — free, thorough,
and it never gives buy or sell calls.
On YouTube,
the most respected educators include CA Rachana Ranade,
a chartered accountant who teaches fundamentals clearly; Pranjal Kamra of Finology,
focused on long-term value investing; and Asset Yogi for financial literacy.
They teach concepts, not calls.
For deeper, more technical learning,
Elearnmarkets by StockEdge and Yadnya Investment Academy offer structured courses on technicals and derivatives.
And to follow seasoned market voices on X, formerly Twitter,
watch fund managers like Samir Arora of Helios,
Saurabh Mukherjea of Marcellus, Nilesh Shah of Kotak,
and Deepak Shenoy of Capitalmind —
for their thinking on the market, not stock tips.
Learn from these; verify everything; and remember that the numbers of subscribers matter far less than whether a creator shows their reasoning.
This is the most important filter of all —
how to tell a real teacher from a tip-seller.
Three tests.
First,
avoid anyone whose main product is specific buy-this-now calls with price targets.
Trust the ones who explain the reasoning behind an idea,
so you can judge it yourself.
A tip makes you dependent; a method makes you independent.
Second,
avoid creators who only appear in roaring bull markets and vanish when it turns,
or who exist mainly to sell you an expensive course on hype.
Trust those who post steadily through bull and bear phases alike.
Third,
avoid anyone who hides their credentials and sources or promises guaranteed returns —
there is no such thing.
Trust those who show who they are,
cite where their facts come from,
and are honest that nothing is guaranteed.
Apply these three tests,
and ninety percent of the noise falls away.
Chapter four, in brief.
Technicals help with when to act; fundamentals decide what to own.
Know trend, support and resistance, volume,
and moving averages.
Do the work in free tools — Screener, Tickertape, Trendlyne —
but treasure the primary sources,
the annual reports and concalls.
Learn from trustworthy channels like Zerodha Varsity,
CA Rachana Ranade, and Pranjal Kamra,
and follow seasoned fund managers for their thinking.
Above all, trust methods over tips, and verify everything.
Now we put research to work — the equity investment strategies.
